- **AI Digital Twin** — https://jouselt.github.io/ai-digital-twin-portfolio/ — ask about his project work and it answers from nine written records, citing the passage behind every claim. When the records do not support an answer it says so and names what is missing instead of guessing. A company that is not in the records is refused before any model loads, because cosine similarity alone cannot tell a covered question from an uncovered one. Angular 20 with the model running in the browser on WebGPU; the page is 75 kB and the 290 MB model only arrives if you ask something. Measured at 14/14 evaluation cases over three runs, with the runs and their caveats committed in the repository. Source: https://github.com/jouselt/ai-digital-twin-portfolio

Fully client-side: Angular 20, no backend, no API key, no account. Scope, honestly: the interview is live today and document generation is still in progress. Source: https://github.com/jouselt/spec-forge

## Case studies

### Commerce API resilience

- **Problem**: a high-traffic commerce API had no isolation between its downstream dependencies. One slow or failing service could take the whole request path down with it, and production problems were hard to attribute.
- **Constraints**: live traffic, no ability to pause the product, an existing test contract that had to keep passing, and a third-party auth library that exposed no timeout option at all.
- **Architecture and depth**: per-backend circuit breakers with opossum across 6 downstream services, an error classification that separates business failures from infrastructure failures, and a fail-fast policy so a broken dependency is cut rather than retried into a cascade. A uniform 10s timeout replaced ad-hoc waits, and the library with no timeout hook was wrapped in a wall-clock cap.
- **Diagnosis and depth**: production hangs of roughly 18 seconds were traced through 99 APM transaction snapshots in AppDynamics. Separately, 63.6% of application logs were found to be misrouting to stdout, narrowed down by comparing 6 APIs until the cause landed in the collection tier: an AWS ECS / Firelens configuration issue.
- **Result**: a backend where a failing dependency degrades predictably instead of cascading, a request path that cannot hang indefinitely, and logs that can be trusted for diagnosis. Observability was built alongside it: a 40+ event typed logging taxonomy, per-request correlation IDs and PII masking, plus Splunk dashboards adopted across 6+ APIs.

### Figma → legacy parity → Stencil pipeline

- **Problem**: a legacy frontend written in PHP was being replaced, and the new component had to preserve behavior that was only documented by the old implementation. Design files described intent; the legacy code described what users actually got. Comparing both by hand, screen by screen, was slow and easy to get wrong.
- **Constraints**: the output had to be a Stencil.js web component reusable across every app, functional parity had to be verifiable rather than assumed, and the migration could not lose features nobody remembered were there.
- **Architecture and depth**: built an AI-assisted pipeline around an MCP server that reads the Figma designs, compares them against the legacy PHP implementation, and converts the result to Stencil. That turned a manual parity audit into a repeatable pass, and it is the mechanism behind the coverage jump on the ported handlers.
- **Key decisions**: treat the legacy code as the specification of record and the design as intent, rather than assuming either one alone was complete. Keep the comparison reproducible so the same pass could be re-run as the component grew.
- **Result**: one Stencil component reusable across all apps, with functional parity against the legacy implementation and handler coverage raised from 9.9% to 100% statements.

### Quick Quote Vista

- **Problem**: Disney needed a quote experience that could serve multiple regions, brands, and responsive breakpoints without fragmenting the implementation.
- **Constraints**: cross-brand consistency, locale-specific variants, booking rules, and enterprise quality expectations under active product evolution.
- **Architecture and depth**: built the component with Stencil.js and Web Component patterns so the same core behavior could be adapted across sites while keeping validation, date selection, and resort selection logic maintainable.
- **Key decisions**: optimized for reuse and predictable responsive behavior instead of per-market one-offs, then cleaned SCSS and expanded test coverage as complexity grew. Change detection optimization and lazy loading cut the initial bundle by 40%.
- **Result**: a multi-variant booking component with 8 international versions serving 20,000+ daily users, bug resolution across breakpoints, and a 40% smaller initial bundle.

### Quick Quote API

- **Problem**: the quote experience needed a backend path that could safely interpret deep-link parameters and drive users into the right destination state.
- **Constraints**: input validation, redirect safety, cookie behavior, and production observability mattered as much as the happy path.
- **Architecture and depth**: designed the endpoint behavior, validation flow, correlation-aware logging, and the Splunk visibility that kept frontend and backend diagnostics traceable. The service ran on Node.js and TypeScript over Restify, behind a BFF layer for commerce APIs.
- **Key decisions**: chose explicit parameter validation and structured diagnostics over opaque redirects to make support and production troubleshooting faster.
- **Result**: a more accountable quote-entry flow with backend diagnostics designed for real operational support, not just feature completion.

### Carnival web ↔ POS payment integration

- **Problem**: Carnival needed the web experience to coordinate securely with POS hardware for payment and signature flows.
- **Constraints**: PCI-sensitive behavior, hardware integration, legacy Verifone compatibility, and support for newer Ingenico devices.
- **Architecture and depth**: implemented WebSocket communication for web ↔ device messaging and helped connect the user-facing payment journey with lower-level device behavior.
- **Key decisions**: optimized for compatibility and reliability under mixed hardware conditions, not just greenfield assumptions.
- **Result**: a working bridge for compliant payment interactions in a complex enterprise environment where correctness mattered more than flashy UI.

## Applied AI differentiator

AI work grounded in software delivery, not novelty. AI is used when it improves engineering discipline: clearer specs, tighter feedback loops, better operational visibility, and workflows teams can actually review.

In practice: Kiro and Claude day to day, MCP-connected tooling, and AI-DLC with Spec Driven Development to keep specs and decisions in the repository instead of in chat history. The clearest example is the Figma-to-legacy parity pipeline: an MCP server doing comparison work that would otherwise have been weeks of manual review.

- **Daily tooling**: Kiro (kiro-cli) and Claude, plus GitHub Copilot occasionally, with MCP integrations reaching the tools the team already uses.
- **AI-DLC**: Inception, Construction, and Operations workflows designed to keep AI output attached to real engineering artifacts.
- **Spec Driven Development (SDD)**: repository-backed specs so context survives beyond a single session or a single person.
- **Honest scope**: strongest fit is applied AI for software teams, product execution, and internal tooling rather than research-heavy ML roles.
